strengths: PST addresses a relevant problem in multimodal NLP: gender stereotypes may change when multiple people and their relationships appear in one image. Studying organizational power alongside occupation is a useful extension.

The occupation experiment systematically crosses 20 male-stereotyped and 20 female-stereotyped occupations in both positional orders. The per-occupation results provide evidence of stereotype adherence beyond selected illustrative examples.

Three human annotators assess each target individual, with reported Fleiss’ kappa of 0.88–0.92. This supports the reliability of perceived-gender labels. Providing descriptor lists, generation templates, and annotation instructions also improves auditability.
weaknesses: The central fairness conclusions exceed what SS establishes. Equation 1 averages signed stereotype adherence, allowing opposing biases to cancel. Table 1 illustrates this: the single-person occupation score of 10 combines female- and male-stereotype scores of 50 and −30. Even the gender-stratified averages can conceal differences between occupations. FairCritic’s aggregate scores near zero therefore do not demonstrate 'near-perfect fairness.' This requires sufficiently sampled, per-identity deviations from gender parity and analysis of joint gender distributions.

The single-versus-paired comparison lacks adequate uncertainty analysis. Only three single-person images are sampled per identity, and the occupation PST experiment has one generation per ordered pair. Consequently, occupation-level amplification estimates and rankings can be sensitive to sampling noise. Organizational-power experiments additionally sample role combinations without clearly establishing matched coverage across conditions. More sampling, explicit matching, and confidence intervals are needed; three samples alone do not ensure statistical significance.

Figure 6 compares events with different baselines: one stereotype-adhering person versus at least one of two people. Independent, gender-balanced generation already produces PST(Any) in 75% of images, so the headline 74.3% requires careful interpretation. The substantial PST(Both) rate is more informative. Numerical reconciliation is also needed: under Equation 1 and common denominators, the reported occupation rates imply SS = 71.9 + 74.3 − 100 = 46.2, rather than Table 1’s 47.38.

FairCritic is insufficiently specified for reproduction. Section 5.1 identifies the critic model and one-loop limit but omits exact critic instructions, image batch sizes, feedback incorporation details, and whether evaluation uses fresh samples independent of feedback construction. Annotation aggregation and handling of 'Cannot Identify' responses are also unclear. The inconsistent totals of 944 versus 1,952 constructed prompts further complicate understanding the evaluated dataset. Promising a later code release does not resolve these methodological omissions.

The evidence does not isolate FairCritic’s advantage over simpler interventions. Table 2 evaluates occupational prompt intervention on the five most biased occupations per gender, whereas Table 1 reports FairCritic across the broader set. A comparison on identical prompts and generation budgets, including a fixed diversity-guidance baseline, is needed. There is also no systematic assessment of person count, role-position adherence, or image quality after mitigation. These validity and reproducibility gaps require important revisions before the paper supports a Findings recommendation.
